newsitem.title: USA: Judge denies Hilton motion for ITT meeting.
newsitem.headline: Judge denies Hilton motion for ITT meeting.

text.p: A federal judge on Monday denied a motion by Hilton Hotels Corp to compel ITT Corp to hold its annual meeting in mid-May, ending Hilton's attempt to force a quick shareholder vote on its $6.5 billion hostile bid for ITT.
"Hilton's motion for a preliminary injunction...is denied," U.S. District Judge Philip Pro wrote at the end of his seven page ruling, a court clerk told Reuters.
Hilton launched its $55 per share, two-step bid for ITT in late January. ITT later rejected the offer as inadequate.
Since then, ITT has said it would focus on its core businesses in hotels and gambling, and it has started selling assets to fend off Hilton's bid.
ITT owns Sheraton brand hotels and Caesars brand casinos. It has sold its stake in a French telecommunications company and agreed to sell Madison Square Garden Inc.
Hilton has launched a proxy contest for control of ITT's board of directors asking ITT shareholders to vote for a Hilton-nominated slate of directors at the next ITT meeting.
But ITT, which traditionally holds its meeting in mid-May, has yet to schedule the conference, arguing in court that its bylaws allow it to hold the meeting as late as mid-November.
Hilton claimed ITT's bylaws and Nevada law require 1997's shareholder gathering no later than one year after 1996's.
Following today's ruling, ITT spokesman Jim Gallagher said the company was "pleased" with the ruling.
"ITT remains on course to deliver superior value for our shareholders by continuing to operate our core lodging and gaming properties, while realizing the full value of our non-core assets," he said.
ITT has yet to determine a date for its 1997 meeting, Gallagher said.
A Hilton spokesman said the company was preparing a statement in reaction to Judge Pro's decision.
In his written ruling, Judge Pro ruled Hilton's argument that an annual meeting, as used in Nevada law and ITT's bylaws, means every twelve months "misapprehends the term."

"The court finds persuasive (an affidavit) that the term annual meeting at issue must be understood as an adjective which distinguishes the regular meeting for the election of directors for other special meetings called by the board for the stockholders."
Judge Pro also wrote that in accordance with Nevada statutes, "ITT's board of directors retains reasonable discretion in setting an annual meeting to resist hostile takeover offers."
